questions.stem: Which party won the 1948 South African election and began introducing apartheid?
options: the National Party
the United Party
the Progressive Party
the Liberal Party
questions.explanation: D. F. Malan's National Party, drawing mainly on Afrikaner voters, won in 1948 and governed until 1994. The United Party of Jan Smuts lost that election.

questions.stem: The ideology behind apartheid, as developed by Hendrik Verwoerd, is best summed up as:
options: 'separate development', with each racial group kept apart under white control
gradual assimilation of all groups into a single non-racial South African nation
equal rights for all citizens combined with separate schools for each language
majority rule with special guarantees for the white minority's property
questions.explanation: Apartheid rested on Afrikaner nationalism and the claim that races should develop separately, which in practice meant white supremacy and the denial of rights to the black majority. Verwoerd, as minister and then prime minister, gave it the language of 'separate development'.

questions.stem: The Population Registration Act of 1950 was fundamental to apartheid because it:
options: set aside separate residential areas in cities for each race
classified every person by race, which then decided their rights
allowed all South Africans to vote in elections for the first time
banned the Communist Party and any group seeking social change
questions.explanation: The Act required everyone to be classified as White, Coloured, Native (later Bantu or Black) or, later, Indian or Asian, and that classification governed where people could live, work, study and marry. Separate residential areas came from the Group Areas Act, also of 1950.

questions.stem: Which apartheid law of 1950 divided towns and cities into separate residential zones for each racial group?
options: the Separate Amenities Act
the Suppression of Communism Act
the Group Areas Act
the Bantu Education Act
questions.explanation: The Group Areas Act led to the forced removal of hundreds of thousands of people from areas declared for whites, such as Sophiatown in Johannesburg and later District Six in Cape Town. The Separate Amenities Act of 1953 segregated public facilities.

questions.stem: What was the purpose of the Bantu Education Act of 1953?
options: to give black and white children the same curriculum in mixed state schools
to make Afrikaans the only language of instruction in every university
to close all mission schools and replace them with free private academies
to give black children a separate, inferior schooling for low-paid work
questions.explanation: The Act brought black schooling under state control with a curriculum designed to prepare students for manual labour, and many mission schools closed rather than accept it. It became a major grievance, later central to the Soweto uprising.

questions.stem: The pass laws were among the most hated parts of apartheid because they:
options: forced black Africans to carry passes controlling where they lived and worked
required all South Africans to pass a literacy test before they could find work
allowed only white South Africans to obtain passports for travel overseas
made black Africans pay a tax each time they passed from one city to another
questions.explanation: Black African men, and from the 1950s women too, had to carry a reference book or pass, and failure to produce it could mean arrest. Hundreds of thousands were prosecuted each year, and passes became the target of major protests, including the one at Sharpeville.

questions.stem: By 1960, which statement best describes the demographic and economic impact of apartheid?
options: Most black South Africans lived in the cities and owned land in proportion to their numbers
A white minority held power while the black majority was confined to about 13 per cent of the land
A black majority held political power while the white minority still controlled most of the country's mines
The races were spread evenly across the land, but voting was limited to those who owned property
questions.explanation: Under the 1913 and 1936 land laws, the African majority was restricted to reserves making up about 13 per cent of the land, while whites, a minority, held political power and most land and wealth. Black workers provided cheap labour for mines, farms and factories under the migrant labour system.

questions.stem: Which organisation, founded in 1912, became the leading national movement against apartheid?
options: the United Democratic Front
the Inkatha Freedom Party
the African National Congress
the Pan Africanist Congress of Azania
questions.explanation: The ANC was founded in 1912 as the South African Native National Congress. The PAC broke away in 1959, the UDF was formed in 1983, and Inkatha was a Zulu-based movement led by Mangosuthu Buthelezi.

questions.stem: How did the ANC Youth League, formed in 1944 by figures such as Nelson Mandela, Walter Sisulu and Oliver Tambo, change the ANC?
options: It pushed the ANC towards mass action such as boycotts, strikes and civil disobedience
It persuaded the ANC to give up politics and focus only on church and welfare work
It ended the ANC's alliance with Indian and coloured groups and adopted armed struggle at once
It led the ANC to support the National Party's policy of separate development
questions.explanation: The Youth League criticised the older leaders' petitions and deputations. Its 1949 Programme of Action committed the ANC to boycotts, strikes and civil disobedience, leading to the Defiance Campaign of 1952. Armed struggle came only in 1961.

questions.stem: During the Defiance Campaign of 1952, volunteers:
options: attacked police stations and government offices in the main cities with explosives
voted in large numbers in elections from which black South Africans were excluded
left South Africa to set up a government in exile in Tanzania and Zambia
broke apartheid laws, such as entering whites-only areas, and accepted arrest
questions.explanation: More than 8,000 volunteers were arrested for nonviolently breaking laws such as curfews, pass laws and segregated facilities. ANC membership grew greatly. Sabotage began only with Umkhonto we Sizwe in 1961.

questions.stem: Why did Robert Sobukwe and others break away from the ANC to form the Pan Africanist Congress in 1959?
options: They wanted to negotiate with the National Party rather than use mass protest against it
They supported apartheid's homelands as the basis for future independent African states
They believed armed struggle should be given up in favour of court cases and petitions
They rejected the ANC's multiracial alliances and wanted Africans to lead alone
questions.explanation: The Africanists objected to the ANC's alliance with white, Indian and coloured organisations and to the Freedom Charter's statement that South Africa belonged to all who lived in it. The PAC stressed African self-reliance. It did not support the homelands or negotiate with the government.

questions.stem: The Freedom Charter was adopted at the Congress of the People held at Kliptown in:
questions.explanation: About 3,000 delegates of the Congress Alliance met at Kliptown, near Johannesburg, on 25-26 June 1955. Police broke up the meeting on its second day.

questions.stem: Which demand was central to the Freedom Charter of 1955?
options: A whites-only parliament with an elected advisory council for each African tribe
A non-racial South Africa in which all people had equal rights and a vote
A separate black state in the Transkei with its own army and currency
An immediate armed uprising led by the ANC against the government
questions.explanation: The Charter called for a non-racial democracy, equal rights before the law, a share in the country's wealth and the end of pass laws and job discrimination. It remained the ANC's guiding document and influenced the 1996 constitution.

questions.stem: What was the outcome of the Treason Trial of 1956-1961?
options: The trial was abandoned when the ANC agreed to disband
None of the 156 accused, including Mandela, was convicted
All 156 accused were sentenced to life on Robben Island
Mandela alone was convicted, and the other accused were all released
questions.explanation: In December 1956 the government arrested 156 leaders of the Congress Alliance and charged them with treason, claiming the Freedom Charter was a communist plot. Charges were gradually dropped, and the last of the accused, including Mandela, were acquitted in March 1961. The trial still tied up the leadership for years.

questions.stem: On 21 March 1960 at Sharpeville, police opened fire on a crowd protesting against the pass laws. What was the result?
options: 69 people were killed, and the government banned the ANC and PAC
6 people were killed, and the government repealed the pass laws
690 people were killed, and South Africa left the United Nations
No one was killed, but Mandela was arrested for organising it
questions.explanation: Police shot dead 69 people at a PAC protest, many shot in the back as they fled. The government declared a state of emergency and banned the ANC and PAC in April 1960. The pass laws remained until 1986.

questions.stem: In 1961 the ANC created Umkhonto we Sizwe (MK). What was its initial strategy?
options: Full-scale guerrilla war launched from bases inside the Bantustans
Mass strikes and boycotts with no use of force of any kind at all
Sabotage of government and economic targets while avoiding loss of life
Assassination of National Party ministers and of senior police officers
questions.explanation: After Sharpeville and the banning of the ANC, leaders including Mandela concluded nonviolence alone could not succeed. MK began on 16 December 1961 with a sabotage campaign against installations such as power lines, intended to avoid casualties.

questions.stem: Why is Sharpeville often seen as a turning point in resistance to apartheid?
options: It convinced the banned movements that peaceful protest alone could not succeed
It persuaded the government to begin negotiations with the ANC within a year
It ended international criticism, because the government successfully blamed the protesters
It caused the PAC and ANC to merge into a single organisation led by Sobukwe
questions.explanation: Sharpeville led to the banning of the ANC and PAC, closing legal avenues of protest, and both turned to armed struggle through MK and Poqo. It also brought international condemnation. Negotiations came only around 1990, and the two organisations stayed separate.

questions.stem: The Rivonia Trial of 1963-64 followed a police raid on Liliesleaf Farm. What was its outcome?
options: Mandela was deported to Britain and forbidden to return home
Mandela and other MK leaders were sentenced to life imprisonment
Mandela was sentenced to death but released after an appeal
The accused were acquitted after the judge found there was no evidence
questions.explanation: Mandela, already in prison, was tried with Walter Sisulu, Govan Mbeki and others for sabotage. They faced a possible death sentence, but in June 1964 eight were sentenced to life imprisonment, and most were sent to Robben Island.

questions.stem: How did Mandela's imprisonment on Robben Island affect the anti-apartheid struggle?
options: It removed him from leadership but made him an international symbol of resistance
It ended his influence, since prisoners were never allowed any visitors or letters
It led the ANC to choose a new strategy of cooperation with the Bantustan leaders
It allowed him to lead MK's sabotage campaign through messages to the guards
questions.explanation: Imprisonment kept Mandela and other leaders out of active politics for decades, but Robben Island became a 'university' for political education, and campaigns such as 'Free Mandela' in the 1980s made him a global symbol. Prisoners had very limited, heavily censored contact, not none at all.

questions.stem: Steve Biko was the best-known leader of which movement?
options: the Defiance Campaign of 1952-53
the United Democratic Front
the Mass Democratic Movement
the Black Consciousness Movement
questions.explanation: Biko helped found the South African Students' Organisation and developed Black Consciousness in the late 1960s and 1970s. He died in police custody in September 1977.

questions.stem: Black Consciousness, as developed by Steve Biko, stressed that:
options: black and white students should merge into a single national student union
black people should accept the Bantustans as the first step to independence
black people must overcome feelings of inferiority and lead their own struggle
black people should rely on white liberals to win reforms through the parliament
questions.explanation: Biko argued that apartheid's psychological effects had to be overcome, and that black people, including Indian and coloured South Africans, should organise themselves rather than depend on white liberal allies. He rejected the Bantustans.

questions.stem: The Soweto Uprising of 16 June 1976 began as a protest by school students against:
options: the release of Nelson Mandela from Robben Island
the creation of the Transkei as an independent state
the use of Afrikaans as a language of instruction
the arrest of Steve Biko and other student leaders
questions.explanation: Students marched against a decree requiring half of certain subjects to be taught in Afrikaans. Police opened fire, killing students including the schoolboy Hector Pieterson, and protests spread across the country. Biko died in custody in 1977, and Mandela was released in 1990.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains the significance of the Soweto Uprising?
options: It marked the end of the Black Consciousness Movement's influence on students
It brought a new generation into the struggle, and many young people joined MK
It ended the Bantu Education system, since the government abolished it soon afterwards
It showed the ANC leadership was in full control of the protests from within prison
questions.explanation: Soweto showed the influence of Black Consciousness on young people and revived mass resistance. Thousands of students left the country, many joining MK, which strengthened the exiled ANC. Bantu Education continued, and the protests were led by students, not the imprisoned leaders.

questions.stem: Which was a key tactic of repression used by South African governments from the 1960s?
options: Detention without trial, banning orders and torture of detainees
Allowing opposition parties to compete freely in national elections
Releasing political prisoners in exchange for promises of loyalty
Granting independent courts the power to overturn security laws
questions.explanation: Laws such as the 90-day detention law of 1963 and the Terrorism Act of 1967 allowed indefinite detention without trial. Banning orders restricted people's movement and speech, and dozens died in detention, Steve Biko among them.

questions.stem: Which evidence best shows the use of state terror by South Africa's security forces in the 1980s?
options: Police units such as the one at Vlakplaas killed activists, as later revealed
Police were required to obtain court warrants before arresting any single protester
The army was confined to barracks during the states of emergency of 1985-86
Security forces were placed under the authority of the ANC from 1983 onwards
questions.explanation: Covert security police units, including the unit based at Vlakplaas, carried out killings of activists, as later evidence, including to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, revealed. States of emergency in 1985 and 1986 gave police and army sweeping powers, and thousands were detained.

questions.stem: Under the Bantustan or homelands policy, the government aimed to:
options: assign black South Africans to ethnic homelands and strip their citizenship
give every black South African a farm in the most fertile parts of the country
merge all homelands into a single black state with a seat at the United Nations
move the white population into homelands and leave the cities to black residents
questions.explanation: The Promotion of Bantu Self-Government Act of 1959 set up ethnic homelands. Transkei (1976), Bophuthatswana (1977), Venda (1979) and Ciskei (1981) were declared 'independent', and their people lost South African citizenship. No other country recognised them.

questions.stem: Why did the international community refuse to recognise the 'independent' Bantustans such as Transkei?
options: They had voted to join neighbouring states such as Botswana and Lesotho instead
They were ruled directly by the ANC from its headquarters in exile
They had refused to hold any elections or appoint any leaders at all
They were seen as a device to deny black South Africans their citizenship
questions.explanation: The UN and other states saw the homelands as a way to make the black majority foreigners in their own country and to entrench apartheid. Their governments were dependent on Pretoria. The homelands were reincorporated into South Africa in 1994.

questions.stem: Forced removals under apartheid are best described as:
options: the movement of millions of people by force to areas assigned by race
the voluntary migration of black workers to jobs in the gold mines
the deportation of white opponents of apartheid to Britain
the transfer of political prisoners from Robben Island to Pretoria
questions.explanation: Under the Group Areas Act, the homelands policy and the clearing of 'black spots', an estimated 3.5 million people were removed between 1960 and the early 1980s. Communities such as Sophiatown and District Six were destroyed.

questions.stem: How did South Africa respond to the independence of Angola and Mozambique in 1975?
options: It intervened militarily and backed rebel movements such as UNITA and RENAMO
It signed defence treaties with both of their new governments against the ANC
It ended apartheid laws in the border regions to win their friendship
It withdrew its forces from Namibia and handed control to the UN
questions.explanation: South Africa saw the new Marxist governments as threats that could shelter the ANC. Its army fought in Angola and backed UNITA, and it supported RENAMO in Mozambique. It also raided ANC bases in neighbouring states. South Africa held Namibia until 1990.

questions.stem: The Nkomati Accord of 1984 between South Africa and Mozambique is an example of:
options: Mozambique agreeing to join South Africa as one of its homelands
Mozambique allowing MK to set up bases in return for South African aid
Pretoria using pressure on a neighbour to make it expel the ANC
Pretoria agreeing to end apartheid in exchange for trade with Mozambique
questions.explanation: Under the accord, Mozambique agreed to stop the ANC operating from its territory, and South Africa promised to stop supporting RENAMO, a promise it did not keep. It shows how destabilisation forced neighbouring Frontline States to limit support for the ANC.

questions.stem: Archbishop Desmond Tutu, a leading church critic of apartheid, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in:
questions.explanation: Tutu received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984 for his nonviolent opposition to apartheid, which drew world attention to the struggle. Mandela and de Klerk shared the prize in 1993.

questions.stem: The United Democratic Front, formed in 1983, changed the nature of resistance because it:
options: united hundreds of local civic, church, youth and union groups in mass protest
was the first organisation ever to call for armed struggle against the government
was a whites-only party that campaigned in parliament for gradual reform
was set up by the government to represent the views of the homeland leaders
questions.explanation: The UDF was launched to oppose the new tricameral parliament, which excluded black Africans. It brought together hundreds of organisations in rent and consumer boycotts, strikes and campaigns to make townships ungovernable, alongside the union federation COSATU from 1985.

questions.stem: Which was an example of international pressure on the apartheid government?
options: The US Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act of 1986, passed over President Reagan's veto
The decision of the UN Security Council in 1977 to recognise the Transkei as a state
The Commonwealth's decision to award South Africa the 1982 Commonwealth Games
The 1985 agreement by foreign banks to lend South Africa more money at lower rates
questions.explanation: Congress passed sanctions in 1986 despite Reagan's preference for 'constructive engagement'. Other pressures included the 1977 mandatory UN arms embargo, sporting boycotts and disinvestment. In 1985 foreign banks, led by Chase Manhattan, refused to roll over loans, causing a financial crisis.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the role of international responses in ending apartheid?
options: Western governments ended apartheid by sending troops to support the ANC in 1989
Sanctions and the debt crisis raised the cost of apartheid, but internal resistance was decisive
International responses were the only cause, because internal resistance had been crushed by 1980
International responses had no effect because South Africa traded only with neighbouring states
questions.explanation: Most historians argue that sanctions, disinvestment and the 1985 debt crisis weakened the economy and isolated the regime, but that mass internal resistance in the 1980s made the country ungovernable. Combined with the end of the Cold War, these pressures pushed the government to negotiate.

questions.stem: On 2 February 1990 President F. W. de Klerk announced:
options: the unbanning of the ANC, PAC and Communist Party and the coming release of Mandela
a new state of emergency and the arrest of all members of the United Democratic Front
the independence of the remaining homelands and the end of their South African citizenship
a whites-only election to choose a new president to replace the ailing P. W. Botha
questions.explanation: In his speech to parliament, de Klerk lifted the bans on the liberation movements and announced Mandela's release, which followed on 11 February 1990. This opened the way to negotiations.

questions.stem: Which combination of factors best explains the collapse of apartheid by the early 1990s?
options: The death of P. W. Botha and a UN invasion that removed the National Party
Mass resistance, economic decline, sanctions and the end of the Cold War
A military defeat of the South African army by MK forces inside the country
A decision by white voters in 1983 to hand power immediately to the ANC
questions.explanation: Internal resistance, a weakening economy, international isolation and the end of the Cold War, which removed the 'communist threat' argument, persuaded de Klerk's government to negotiate. MK never defeated the army, and Botha was replaced after a stroke in 1989, not killed.

questions.stem: In the March 1992 referendum, white voters:
options: backed further negotiations to end apartheid, by about two-thirds
rejected negotiations, forcing de Klerk to resign the presidency
voted to restore the pass laws that had been repealed in 1986
voted to create a separate Afrikaner state in the Orange Free State
questions.explanation: About 69 per cent of white voters supported de Klerk's reform process, strengthening his hand against the right wing. Talks continued despite later crises.

questions.stem: Which problem most threatened the transition to democracy between 1990 and 1994?
options: The decision of the National Party to boycott all negotiations from 1991
Violence, including ANC-Inkatha clashes and the assassination of Chris Hani
The refusal of the ANC to take part in any election that was held before the year 2000
An invasion by Zimbabwe aimed at installing its own candidate as president
questions.explanation: Thousands died in political violence, much of it between ANC and Inkatha supporters, with evidence of security force involvement. The killing of SACP leader Chris Hani by a right-wing extremist in April 1993 brought the country close to crisis, but Mandela's appeal for calm helped keep talks on track.

questions.stem: In the election of April 1994:
options: only white and coloured citizens voted, and black South Africans voted the following year
the ANC won about 62 per cent, and Mandela led a Government of National Unity
the National Party won a majority and de Klerk remained president until the year 2000
the ANC and PAC formed a coalition after neither party won more than 30 per cent of the vote
questions.explanation: South Africa's first democratic election, with all adults voting, gave the ANC about 62 per cent. Mandela was inaugurated on 10 May 1994, with de Klerk and Thabo Mbeki as deputy presidents in a Government of National Unity.

questions.stem: Joe Slovo's 'sunset clauses' of 1992 helped the negotiations by proposing that:
options: the ANC give up its demand for one person, one vote in return for land
the homelands become independent states in a loose federal union
power be shared for a period, with jobs for existing public servants protected
the white minority keep a permanent veto over all future laws and all new taxes
questions.explanation: Slovo, an ANC and Communist Party leader, proposed temporary power-sharing and guarantees for white civil servants, police and soldiers. This reassured the National Party and helped produce the Government of National Unity, without a permanent white veto.
